newsitem.title: USA: AT&T sets Internet commerce service.
newsitem.headline: AT&T sets Internet commerce service.

text.p: AT&T Corp. Tuesday stepped up its efforts to become a major player on the Internet, offering secure transactions for consumers and easy-to-use tools for businesses marketing products on the World Wide Web.

AT&T offered a suite of products for Internet commerce, most significantly a promise to cover any losses consumers suffer on unauthorised transactions. The growth of Internet business has been retarded by widespread consumer worries over security.

"Having the trust of AT&T backing the security of those transactions, just as it has with its telephone network, will go a long way toward allaying people's fears," said Peter Bernstein of Infonautics Consulting in Ramsey, N.J.

AT&T also addressed another concern of Internet users: The difficulty of learning new technology. AT&T unveiled a "turnkey" solution to maintain Web sites for business, requiring no technical knowledge on the part of users.
AT&T Chairman Robert Allen, who led the launch, said the products would make doing business on the Internet as easy as dialing an 800 toll-free telephone number.
"AT&T revolutionised business with the invention of 800- toll-free service, and we intend to do no less for Web-based commerce," Allen said in a statement.

The nation's biggest long-distance phone company said it would offer a service to allow businesses to build and maintain sites on the Internet's popular World Wide Web as well as provide ways to attract customers to the site.

For the telephone giant, the move into this new business is critical. Its main long-distance business is under attack from all sides, as deregulation allows more and more competitors into the business.

By building its Internet business, it will be "adding minutes to its network," said Christopher Landes of Telechoice, a Verona, N.J.-based consultant, with data volume replacing the loss of long distance calls.
AT&T's move to provide Internet security met with some criticism from rivals in the computer industry, who complained that the guarantees give undue credence to fears about credit card fraud.

An official at International Business Machines Corp.'s electronic commerce business unit noted that consumers were already protected by credit card issuers against fradulent claims made on their credit cards over $50.
"IBM doesn't feel offering additional insurance is the way to make people feel more confident" about carrying out transactions over the Internet, the official said.
In addition, the IBM manager said, the AT&T system locks merchants into a proprietary system of software that makes them dependent on AT&T for a vital part of their business.

AT&T made a major splash earlier this year by offering up to five hours a month of free Internet access, but the marketing plan became an embarrassment when its circuits were overloaded with requests for the service. Analysts say it signed up over 500,000 users this year, making it a leader in Internet access.
The services unveiled Tuesday are aimed at consumers as well as business users, most of whom now to view the Internet and the Web as marketing, rather than sales tools.
AT&T said it was hoping to change that view.
Allen said the company's new service would attract customers and "turn (Web) browsers into buyers."

Under its programme, AT&T said it would guarantee secure Internet transactions for Web shoppers who join the company's free Secure Buyer's programme and charge their Internet purchases to their AT&T Universal credit cards.

The company said that regardless of which Internet access provider consumers use, Web shoppers will not have to pay for purchases by unauthorised users. AT&T itself offers Internet access through its Worldnet service.

AT&T also said merchants buying its Secure Buy service would not miss an order. It said it would refund the amount of a sale, up to the monthly Secure Buy service fee of $395 to $595 a month, if an order did not reach a merchant.
It also said it would guarantee that customers using its service would never have their Web sites give the message "server not available," which is similar to a busy signal.
AT&T's stock closed at $39.375, down 62.5 cents a share, on the New York Stock Exchange.
